content: Nicocodeine, marketed under brand names such as Lyopect® and Tusscodin®, is an opiate derivative that is chemically related to dihydrocodeine. It is the codeine analogue of nicomorphine and was developed for use as a cough suppressant and analgesic. However, it is not widely used in most countries. Its pharmacological activity is comparable to that of other opiates. Nicocodeine and nicomorphine were first introduced in the late 1950s by Lannacher Heilmittel, a pharmaceutical company based in Austria. Once administered, nicocodeine undergoes hepatic metabolism through demethylation, converting it into nicomorphine, also known as 6-nicotinoylmorphine. Nicomorphine is then further metabolized into morphine, which is responsible for its pharmacological effects. The side effects of nicocodeine are similar to those observed with other opiates. These include pruritus (itching), nausea, and respiratory depression, which can be life-threatening in cases of overdose or misuse. In terms of regulation, nicocodeine is controlled in a manner similar to codeine and other weak opiates, such as ethylmorphine, benzylmorphine, and dihydrocodeine, as well as their derivatives like acetyldihydrocodeine. However, it is not regulated in the same category as stronger opiates like hydrocodone or oxycodone, which are classified similarly to morphine. Nicocodeine is also subject to international drug control laws, including the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. In the United States, nicocodeine is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, placing it in the same category as heroin. This classification reflects the fact that nicocodeine was never approved for medical use in the United States. A related compound, nicodicodeine, is structurally similar to nicocodeine in the same way that codeine is related to dihydrocodeine. When metabolized, nicodicodeine produces dihydromorphine, whereas nicocodeine is metabolized into morphine, as previously described. Nicocodeine is available in various pharmaceutical formulations. For cough suppression, it is commonly prepared as syrups, extended-release syrups, and sublingual drops. For pain relief, it is available as sublingual drops and oral tablets. Its potency is approximately equivalent to that of hydrocodone. The CAS (Chemical Abstracts Service) number for nicocodeine hydrochloride is 58263-01-7.
